blocks.text:
This programme is designed as a private journey with premium service. The core package includes English-speaking guides, transfers and a guided excursion programme. Free days in Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Aires can be tailored with additional experiences: helicopter flights, island trips, cooking workshops, food and wine tours, a gaucho ranch or an excursion to Uruguay.

In Rio, the main sights bring together dramatic heights and the ocean. Sugarloaf Mountain and Corcovado reveal a city set between granite peaks, forest, a bay and the Atlantic. Iguazu offers two very different perspectives: from Brazil, wide panoramas of the cascades; from Argentina, walkways and upper trails that bring you close to the water. Buenos Aires replaces those natural landscapes with architecture, old neighbourhoods, tango, steaks and wine.

## What defines the journey

The premium approach centres on private logistics and the freedom to adjust how much you do on individual days. The principal excursions are already included in the programme, while Rio and Buenos Aires leave room for personal choices.

In Rio, you can add a boat trip to Angra dos Reis, a helicopter flight, a live music and dance show, a caipirinha-making workshop, a churrasco cooking class, the Botanical Garden or a hike up Sugarloaf Mountain.

At Iguazu, the main waterfall excursion can be complemented by the Bird Park and Macuco Safari. The Brazilian side offers a sweeping view of the falls; the Argentine side brings you closer to individual cascades along three different trails.

In Buenos Aires, turn a free day into a culinary tour, spend it on a gaucho ranch or cross the Río de la Plata to Montevideo.

## How the experiences change along the route

Rio first unfolds through its panoramic viewpoints. From Sugarloaf, you look out over the bay, boats, Botafogo, Copacabana, Ipanema, the Rio–Niterói Bridge and forested slopes. Corcovado presents the same city from another mountain ridge. From here, it is especially clear how Rio fits between mountains and ocean, with neighbourhoods climbing hillsides and curving around green expanses.

The city experience is not confined to its viewpoints. The centre has colonial façades, the Cathedral, the Selarón Steps and the historic Confeitaria Colombo. Open since 1894, this café, with its high ceilings, stained glass and mirrors in carved frames, offers a glimpse of a very different Rio, much closer to the late 19th century than to beachside Copacabana.

Food is a separate highlight of the itinerary. At Fogo de Chão, discover Brazil through churrasco. At Marius Degustare, the focus turns to seafood, including shrimp, oysters and fish. For visitors who want to take part in preparing a meal, there are two workshops: making caipirinhas with cachaça, lime and ice, and preparing churrasco over an open fire.

A free day in Rio can be spent entirely outside the city. A schooner cruise around Angra dos Reis passes between green islands, stopping for swims in emerald waters. Dolphins, turtles and rays can be seen in this area. A buffet lunch with fish and seafood is served on an island, with time afterwards for a walk and shopping.

The evening show reveals another side of Rio. It begins with a live orchestra and samba before moving into capoeira. Fast movements, acrobatics and martial arts elements unfold to music. Dinner can be added if you wish. The programme lasts approximately four hours.

A helicopter flight is for those who want to see Rio as one complete geographical panorama. From above, you can understand the distances between Copacabana, Ipanema, Guanabara Bay, the Rio–Niterói Bridge and Corcovado. The contrast between dense urban neighbourhoods, Tijuca Forest, granite summits and the Atlantic is particularly striking.

The Botanical Garden offers a more relaxed day. It contains around 7,000 plant species, avenues of imperial palms, giant Victoria water lilies, pau-brasil trees and an extensive orchid collection. Founded in 1808, the garden is a place to spend several hours among lakes, paths and tropical greenery while remaining within the city.

At Iguazu, the scale suddenly shifts from urban scenery to nature. On the Brazilian side, you mainly view the line of cascades across the canyon and gradually approach the Devil’s Throat. On the Argentine side, routes follow upper and lower levels, while the walkway to the Devil’s Throat brings you directly to the edge where the water plunges into a narrow gorge.

Macuco Safari turns watching the waterfalls into a physical experience. After a ride through the forest, board a motorboat and head towards the cascades. The spray soon becomes a solid wall of water, and the roar grows louder than the engine. The Bird Park, by contrast, offers a short walk among brightly coloured macaws, toucans and parrots in large aviaries.

Buenos Aires brings you back to city life after Iguazu, but the atmosphere changes completely. Instead of the ocean and tropical forest, there are wide avenues, Plaza de Mayo, the Casa Rosada, La Boca and San Telmo. In the evening, a tango show brings together a live orchestra, dinner, Argentine wine and the dance that grew from the port districts to become a national symbol.

There are three different ways to spend a free day in Buenos Aires. The first centres on food and wine; the second on the Argentine pampas and gaucho culture; the third adds another country to your journey. A day ferry trip to Montevideo introduces Uruguay through Independence Square, Palacio Salvo, the old market, museums and free time in the city.

## Additional details of the premium experience

In Rio, a free day can be built around gastronomy. A caipirinha-making workshop takes place on a hotel rooftop overlooking the city. Guided by a bartender, you mix sugarcane cachaça, lime, sugar and ice, taste the cocktail and adjust the balance of flavours. The session ends with a tasting against a backdrop of the ocean and the city skyline.

The churrasco workshop takes a different approach. You cook different cuts of meat on skewers over an open fire, paying attention to heat and doneness. Corn, cheese, bread rolls and cinnamon-dusted fruit are also prepared over the flames. Afterwards, everyone sits down to dinner and tastes what they have just cooked.

For an active day, choose a hike up Sugarloaf Mountain. The first section follows a forest trail to Urca and takes around 30 minutes. The second requires an instructor and specialist equipment: the route becomes more exposed and includes elements of climbing. It is an option for those seeking more than the usual cable-car ascent.

Rio’s restaurant recommendations cover several neighbourhoods and styles. Gero Trattoria in Ipanema serves Italian and European cuisine. Oro in Leblon focuses on contemporary Brazilian cooking and local ingredients. Satyricon in Ipanema specialises in seafood. Aprazível in Santa Teresa pairs Brazilian cuisine with open-air terraces and city views. Other recommended venues on selected days include Cipriani, Fogo de Chão, Al Mare and Marius Degustare.

In Buenos Aires, a food tour centres on meat, open-fire cooking, desserts with dulce de leche and wine. An optional culinary excursion lets you compare different Argentine cuts and degrees of doneness before moving on to desserts and a wine tasting. This programme lasts approximately six hours.

A ranch visit provides a different context for Argentine cuisine. Guests are first welcomed with empanadas and wine in a pulpería. At 13:00, an asado begins, with different meats, salads and drinks. After lunch, enjoy a folk show, dancing and gaucho displays of horsemanship and lasso skills. The return to Buenos Aires is scheduled for 16:30.

Restaurant recommendations in Buenos Aires focus on Palermo and Puerto Madero. Fogón Asado and La Carnicería specialise in steaks and Argentine cooking. Cabaña Las Lilas and La Cabaña are in Puerto Madero. Piegari combines Italian, European and Argentine cuisines. Crystal Bar is on the 35th floor of Alvear Icon and is recommended above all for its view over the city.

In every city, you can leave free time between the principal excursions and dinners.
